ts2l2nl99d: ## Defender for Office 365: audit before activating
25vdjnv62dd: The documented flow begins with three audits: the **public MX record**, the **accepted domains** and the **inbound connectors**. They determine where email actually enters: if a third-party service filters email before Exchange Online, the protections do not see the message in the same way. Next come activating the evaluation, creating **pilot groups**, configuring protection and trying the capabilities. The full deployment extends the groups until all mailboxes are covered.
1glpz8muzpg: Classic trap: configuring policies without having verified the email path. Auditing the MX avoids hours of troubleshooting on “Safe Links does nothing” when traffic does not arrive through the expected service.
j0f2qrww7k: ## Defender for Identity: sensors and logs
14hl8pngr01: The flow: configure the **instance**, install and configure the **sensors**, set the **event log** and the **proxy** on the machines that carry a sensor, then let Defender for Identity **identify local administrators** on the other machines. The pilot is done on a subset of servers, then steps 2 to 4 are repeated on the remaining servers. A missing or unhealthy sensor = a blind spot on the on-premises Active Directory, and module 8 comes back to it.
2112ubm14qy: ## Defender for Cloud Apps: connect, integrate, discover
17kmyrkwrot: The documented flow: connect, **integrate Defender for Endpoint** (which feeds application discovery from devices), deploy a **log collector** on firewalls and proxies, create a pilot group, discover and manage applications, configure **conditional access app control**, apply **session policies**. 1bfz7g0e5d3: The timeline is the source of facts: processes launched, files created, network connections. It shows what the sensor observed, not necessarily everything that happened. 2g9w2f59thk: **Live response** opens a remote shell connection on the device to collect forensic data, run scripts, send entities to analysis, remediate and hunt. 1o2d4qrk33b: ## High-value assets: limit what the console can do
11et7w18tyj: Some high-impact actions can be **restricted** on high-value assets to avoid a business interruption. The documentation groups the capabilities into four families: **basic response** (scan, file collection, package), **advanced response** (isolate, restrict execution, request remediation), **live response** and **device protection** (automated investigation). When a device is onboarded with a “restricted mode” package, the allowed actions are **defined at onboarding and cannot be changed remotely**. Devices onboarded in restricted mode **do not support running live response scripts**, by design, even if live response is enabled. Detection, alerts and sensor coverage are not affected.

ffe3jpulzx: ## Sheet: groups, EDR in block mode, tampering
b747rbh9y0: - Tags: context; groups: rule, rank, remediation, access.
1mlunggxp2i: - EDR in block mode: Plan 2, third-party antivirus in passive; without real-time, network, ASR, indicators.
19171brn0zi: - Tamper: blocks changes and exclusions; a tool may appear to succeed; troubleshooting mode.
fj8q84r7tj: **Tags** are labels that carry business context (department, location, criticality); all users see the tagged devices. On their own, they control neither access nor policies. **Device groups** build on them: matching rule (name, domain, tags, platform), **automated remediation level** and **Entra user groups** with access. **Dynamic** tags (asset management rules) update roughly every hour; **manual** tags suit ad hoc use.
250spf3aswy: - up to **2,000 groups** per tenant; you must be a Security Administrator to manage them;
azxbjja84f: - if a device matches several groups, it is added only to the **highest-ranked group** (rank 1 = highest priority);
1og51r1o6mc: - a device with no match goes into **Ungrouped devices** (fixed rank, cannot be deleted, but its remediation level and access can be modified);
2d39ok7tqy0: - a group **without a user group** is accessible to everyone with portal access;
ghnbceizyw: - changes can take from a few minutes to several hours;
qkmb3zerws: - deleting a group removes that group from the email notification rules, and deletes the rule if it was the only one.
kcn7kvj43y: Remediation levels: no automated response; semi-automatic with approval for all folders, for non-temporary folders or for system folders; **full remediation**. Microsoft recommends **Full - remediate threats automatically**, unless there is a reason otherwise.
vy5irling4: **EDR in block mode** (Plan 2) acts when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is **not** the primary antivirus and runs in **passive mode**: it fixes malicious artifacts detected after the fact by the EDR, which the third-party antivirus may have missed. Important limits: without active mode, **real-time protection**, **network protection**, **ASR rules** and **indicators** (file, IP, URL, certificate) are **not** available. The third-party product must provide them. Verification: `Get-MpComputerStatus | select AMRunningMode` returns `Normal`, `Passive` or `EDR Block Mode`. Disabling the feature can take up to 30 minutes.
1bswhvkcc40: On Windows Server, Defender Antivirus does **not** enter passive mode automatically: you set the `ForceDefenderPassiveMode` key (DWORD = 1) **before** onboarding. With tamper protection, you can switch to active mode but not go back to passive mode.
hzex7l57it: When enabled, it prevents changes to essential settings: real-time protection, behavior monitoring, cloud protection, security intelligence updates, automatic actions on threats, and the **exclusions** (not modifiable). Attempts to modify through the registry are blocked. Trap: a change pushed by a management tool or a group policy can **appear to succeed** while the protection blocks it. To change a protected setting, you use **troubleshooting mode**, which is temporary. Never disable, stop or modify the `WinDefend`, `MsSense`, `Sense`, `MsMpEng`, `wscsvc` or `SecurityHealthService` services.

2413yn8q07w: Microsoft Defender Antivirus combines several layers: lightweight machine learning models on the workstation, local behavioral analysis (file-based and fileless threats), detection by signatures and heuristics, then **cloud protection** when the client needs more information. In that case, **metadata** about the file is sent to the service, often with a verdict within a few milliseconds. The documentation specifies that the payload is small, contains no personal data and that file names are hashed. The query can be **synchronous** (the file does not open before the verdict) or **asynchronous**.
23rwaiuyrsw: If the verdict remains uncertain, the service can request a **sample**. The consent setting decides what happens:
1c0x4pa3hr7: - **Send safe samples automatically** (default): automatic sending of samples judged unlikely to contain personal data (for example `.bat`, `.scr`, `.dll`, `.exe`); the user is prompted for consent for the others;
85cht59hl3: - **Always prompt**: consent requested each time (unavailable on macOS and Linux);
fs00q0qjzx: - **Send all samples automatically**: all samples; required to include macros embedded in Word documents;
11d87bleomu: - **Do not send**: no samples; metadata is still sent for detections.
